name: Zdzisław Beksiński
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Beksiński studied architecture (1947–1952) and returned to Sanok in 1955 at age 26, joining the Polish Photographic Society. His first notable exhibition (Pokaz zamknięty) came in 1959 at age 30, and his first museum purchase was in 1964 at age 35.
family_context_summary: Beksiński came from a family linked to Sanok for generations; his great-grandfather founded a boiler manufacturing plant and his grandfather was a locally renowned architect. His father urged him to study architecture.
parent_family_domain_summary: His grandfather was a locally renowned architect credited with many construction designs, and his father was a soldier. The family had manufacturing roots in Sanok.

name: Cesária Évora
milestone_by_age_26: Released her first vinyl recordings in 1964 (age 23), including the single 'Segredo de um coração' on the Casa Mimosa label, and was a headliner at Café Royal in Mindelo with radio broadcasts on Radio Mindelo from the early 1960s.
early_history_summary: Born into poverty in Mindelo, Cape Verde, Évora's father (a violinist) died when she was 7, and she was raised in an orphanage. She began singing morna in local bars at age 16, encouraged by a guitarist. By her early 20s she was performing on Radio Mindelo and had a mentor, Gregório Gonçalves (Ti Goy), who guided her from age 15. Her early 1960s radio recordings were released as singles on the Cape Verdean label Casa Mimosa.
family_context_summary: Born into deep poverty in Mindelo; her father was a violinist who died when she was 7, and her mother was a cook and maid. She was placed in an orphanage as a child because the family could not support her.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her father was a violinist, providing early musical exposure, though he died when she was young. No evidence of sustained parental musical mentorship.
primary_early_advantage_tags: poverty, orphanage, port town nightlife, early performing, mentor Ti Goy, voice talent
evidence_summary: Évora grew up in extreme poverty in Mindelo, Cape Verde, losing her violinist father at age 7 and being placed in an orphanage. She began singing professionally at 16 in local bars, mentored by Gregório Gonçalves from age 15. Mindelo's status as an international port town gave her access to lively nightlife venues. By the early 1960s (age ~20), she was performing on Radio Mindelo and had released vinyl singles on the Casa Mimosa label by 1964 (age 23). Her international fame came decades later, in 1988 at age 47, but her early professional career with radio recordings and singles constitutes a material milestone by 26.

name: Alexei Alexeyevich Abrikosov
milestone_by_age_26: Defended his PhD (Candidate of Science) thesis under Lev Landau at the Institute for Physical Problems in 1951 (age 23), and in 1951–1952 (age 23–24) discovered Type II superconductors and the Abrikosov vortex lattice, one of the most fundamental results in condensed matter physics.
early_history_summary: Born in Moscow to physician parents, Abrikosov entered Moscow State University's physics department in 1945 at age 17. He passed Lev Landau's notoriously difficult 'theoretical minimum' exams at age 19, graduated summa cum laude in 1948, and became Landau's PhD student at the Institute for Physical Problems. He defended his thesis in 1951 and immediately began the work on superconductivity that would earn him the Nobel Prize.
family_context_summary: Born into a prominent Moscow family: his father was vice president of the Academy of Medical Sciences and performed Lenin's autopsy; his mother was a well-known pathologist. His uncle was the Russian Empire's last envoy to Japan. The family had established a confectionary that served the czar's family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were both physicians, providing a scientifically literate household, though not directly in physics. The family's social prominence in Soviet science and medicine provided access to elite educational institutions.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Landau mentor, Moscow State University, Institute for Physical Problems, theoretical minimum, physician parents, Soviet physics center
evidence_summary: Abrikosov was born into a prominent Soviet medical-scientific family in Moscow, giving him access to elite education. He entered Moscow State University at 17, passed Landau's theoretical minimum at 19, and became Landau's PhD student at the Institute for Physical Problems. By 23 he had his PhD and by 24 had discovered Type II superconductors and the vortex lattice—a result that would earn him the 2003 Nobel Prize. Moscow was a world center for theoretical physics, and Landau was one of the greatest physicists of the 20th century, providing extraordinary mentorship.

name: Claudio Abbado
milestone_by_age_26: Won the international Serge Koussevitzky Conducting Competition at the Tanglewood Music Festival in 1958 (age 25), a major prize that launched his international career and led to conducting engagements across Italy and the US.
early_history_summary: Born into a deeply musical Milanese family—his father was a violinist and professor at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory, and his mother was a pianist—Abbado grew up attending performances at La Scala. He entered the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory at 16, then studied conducting at the Chigiana Academy in Siena and the Vienna Academy of Music under Hans Swarowsky. In 1958, the year of his graduation from Vienna, he won the Koussevitzky Prize at Tanglewood, which propelled him to fame.
family_context_summary: Abbado was born into a wealthy and respected Milanese family with deep musical roots. His father was a professional violinist and professor at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory, his mother was an adept pianist, and his older brother Marcello became a concert pianist and composer. The family's musical lineage stretched back generations.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was a violinist and professor at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory who served as his first piano teacher. His mother was also a pianist. His brother Marcello became a concert pianist and director of the Rossini Conservatory. The family was deeply embedded in Milan's musical establishment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: musical family, La Scala immersion, conservatory, Vienna Academy, Swarowsky, Koussevitzky Prize, Milan opera world
evidence_summary: Abbado grew up in a deeply musical Milanese family: his father was a violin professor at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory and his mother was a pianist. He attended La Scala performances and rehearsals from youth, providing direct immersion in one of the world's great opera centers. He trained at the Giuseppe Verdi Conservatory, the Chigiana Academy, and the Vienna Academy of Music under Hans Swarowsky. In 1958 at age 25, he won the Koussevitzky Conducting Competition at Tanglewood, a major international prize that launched his career. His brother Marcello was also a noted musician, and his nephew Roberto became a conductor.

name: Ludovico Einaudi
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Einaudi obtained his composition diploma in 1982 (age 26–27) and received a Tanglewood scholarship the same year, but these are educational achievements. His first significant compositions ('Sul filo d'Orfeo') came in 1984 (age 28–29) and his first solo album 'Le Onde' in 1996 (age 40–41).
family_context_summary: Einaudi was born into a prominent Italian family: his father Giulio Einaudi was a major publisher working with Italo Calvino and Primo Levi, and his paternal grandfather Luigi Einaudi was President of Italy (1948–1955). His mother was an amateur pianist, and his maternal grandfather was a pianist, opera conductor, and composer.
parent_family_domain_summary: His mother played piano and his maternal grandfather was a pianist, opera conductor, and composer, providing musical exposure. His father was a prominent publisher and his grandfather was President of Italy, indicating a high-status family with cultural capital.

name: Tadao Ando
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Ando was a self-taught architect who spent his early twenties traveling and studying buildings in Japan, Europe, and Africa. He established his architectural practice in 1969 (age 28) and completed his first notable building in 1973 (age 32).
family_context_summary: Ando was born in Osaka and raised by his great-grandmother in a 50-square-meter row house. He spent time in a neighborhood of craftsmen, building things from scrap wood as a child. He worked as a boxer before turning to architecture.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as providing architectural or design domain advantage. His neighborhood of craftsmen provided informal exposure to making things.

name: Agnès Varda
milestone_by_age_26: Became the official photographer of the Théâtre National Populaire in Paris in 1951 (age 23), a significant professional position she held for a decade. At age 26 (1954), she shot her first feature film, La Pointe Courte, now regarded as the first film of the French New Wave.
early_history_summary: Born in Brussels to a French mother and Greek refugee father, Varda moved to France during WWII. She studied art history at the École du Louvre and photography at the Vaugirard School, then became a photographer at the Avignon Festival (1948) and the Théâtre National Populaire (1951–1961). Her father bought her a studio on rue Daguerre. At age 26, with no film school training, she shot La Pointe Courte, edited by Alain Resnais and praised by Cahiers du Cinéma.
family_context_summary: Varda was born to an engineer father and a French mother in Brussels. The family fled to Sète, France during WWII. Her father bought her dilapidated shops on rue Daguerre in Paris in 1951, which became her home, studio, and laboratory—a material financial platform for her early career.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her father was an engineer, and there is no evidence of family connections in photography or film. However, her father's purchase of her studio-laboratory was a direct financial platform for her creative work.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Paris, TNP photographer, Jean Vilar, rue Daguerre studio, Alain Resnais, French New Wave, École du Louvre
evidence_summary: Varda grew up in Belgium and France, studying art history at the École du Louvre and photography at the Vaugirard School. Her father bought her a studio-laboratory on rue Daguerre in 1951, providing a material financial platform. Jean Vilar hired her as official photographer of the Théâtre National Populaire from 1951 to 1961, giving her direct professional immersion in Paris's cultural world. She was embedded in the circle of Alain Resnais, Chris Marker, and the emerging French New Wave. At age 26, with no film training, she shot La Pointe Courte, now considered the first French New Wave film. Paris in the 1950s was the center of global cinema culture.

name: Carlos Kleiber
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Kleiber was a répétiteur at the Gärtnerplatz Theatre in Munich from 1952 (age 22) and made his conducting debut at the Potsdam theatre in 1954 (age 24) under the pseudonym Karl Keller. His first significant post as Kapellmeister at the Deutsche Oper am Rhein came in 1958 (age 28). The early conducting debut at a small regional theatre under a pseudonym does not constitute a material milestone.
family_context_summary: Kleiber was born in Berlin to the eminent Austrian conductor Erich Kleiber and American mother Ruth Goodrich. The family emigrated to Buenos Aires in 1935. His father actively discouraged him from pursuing music, leading Carlos to study chemistry at ETH Zurich before switching to music.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father Erich Kleiber was one of the most eminent conductors of the 20th century, chief conductor of the Berlin Staatsoper. Despite actively discouraging Carlos from music, the household provided deep musical immersion. His father's scores and bowings were later studied religiously by Carlos.

name: George Andrew Olah
milestone_by_age_26: Received his doctorate from the Technical University of Budapest in 1949 (age 22) and became a research assistant and then faculty member under Professor Geza Zemplen. By the early 1950s (age 23–26), he had published research on organofluorine chemistry and developed a practical process for producing the heart medication digoxin that was used for years in Hungary.
early_history_summary: Born in Budapest to a lawyer father with no family science background, Olah entered the Technical University of Budapest in 1945 after WWII. He fell in love with chemistry and became a research assistant to Professor Geza Zemplen, a student of Emil Fischer. Despite limited post-war facilities, he pioneered organofluorine chemistry from a makeshift 'balcony laboratory.' He earned his doctorate in 1949 and was a faculty member by the early 1950s, joining the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1954.
family_context_summary: Olah was born into a middle-class Budapest family; his father was a lawyer and his mother was a homemaker. No family members had any interest in science. He received a solid humanities-focused education at a prestigious Gymnasium run by the Piarist Fathers.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family science background whatsoever. His father was a lawyer. The family provided a middle-class education but no domain-specific advantage in chemistry.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Zemplen mentor, Technical University Budapest, balcony laboratory, organofluorine chemistry, post-war Hungary, digoxin process
evidence_summary: Olah grew up in a middle-class Budapest family with no science background, receiving a humanities-focused education. He entered university in 1945 after WWII and fell in love with chemistry, becoming a research assistant to Professor Geza Zemplen (a student of Emil Fischer). Despite severely limited post-war facilities, he pioneered organofluorine chemistry from a makeshift 'balcony laboratory' and earned his doctorate by age 22 in 1949. His early research produced a practical process for the heart medication digoxin used for years in Hungary. The difficult conditions of post-war Hungary, while not a frontier ecosystem, forced resourcefulness and self-reliance.

name: Teresa Teng
milestone_by_age_26: Began her professional singing career in 1967 (age 14) with her first album release, TV hosting role, and record contract. By 1968 (age 15), she achieved widespread fame in Taiwan through 'The Gathering of Stars' TV program. By age 26 (1979), she was a dominant pop star across Asia with multiple hit albums, concerts in Southeast Asia, and recordings in multiple languages.
early_history_summary: Born into a poverty-stricken military family in Taiwan, Teng began voice lessons at age 6 through her father's Air Force contact. She won her first major prize at age 11 (1964) singing at a Broadcasting Corporation of China event. At 14, she dropped out of school to pursue singing professionally, signed with Yeu Jow Records, released her first album, and hosted a TV show. She became famous across Taiwan by 15 and expanded across Asia throughout the 1970s, performing for military audiences and releasing hit albums in multiple languages.
family_context_summary: Teng was born into a poverty-stricken Kuomintang military family in Taiwan, the only daughter among five children. Her father was a soldier who retired in 1957 and sold cakes to make ends meet. The family lived in military dependents' villages. Despite poverty, her parents were music lovers who exposed her to Peking opera and Huangmei opera.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her father was a Peking opera enthusiast and her mother appreciated Huangmei opera, taking Teng to Chinese movie theatres and opera houses. Her father's Air Force connections provided her first voice teacher (an Air Force band instructor) and her first performing audiences (military audiences).
primary_early_advantage_tags: voice lessons age 6, military audiences, talent prize age 11, professional at 14, TV fame at 15, poverty, martial law Taiwan, multilingual
evidence_summary: Teng was born into a poverty-stricken military family in Taiwan but showed extraordinary vocal talent from childhood. Her father's Air Force connections provided her first voice teacher at age 6 and her first performing audiences (military). She won her first major prize at 11, dropped out of school at 14 to sing professionally, and released her first album and hosted a TV show in 1967. By 15, she was famous across Taiwan. The combination of remarkable voice, early specialization, direct audience immersion (nightclubs, TV, radio, military performances), and the expanding Asian pop market made her a dominant star by her mid-twenties. Her family's poverty and the martial-law context created urgency and a distinctive performing niche.

name: Santiago Calatrava
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Calatrava graduated as an architect from the Polytechnic University of Valencia in 1974 (age 23) and was studying structural engineering at ETH Zurich by age 26. He received his PhD from ETH in 1979 (age 28) and established his firm in 1981 (age 30). No built work or significant professional recognition by age 26.
family_context_summary: Calatrava was born in Benimàmet, near Valencia, the youngest of five siblings. His father encouraged his artistic tendencies but died when Calatrava was 12. He was then sent to live with his uncle's family. From age 8 he studied art, and from age 13 he spent summers with a Swiss family learning French and German.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father encouraged his artistic tendencies. The family had an old aristocratic surname (Calatrava) associated with a medieval order of knights, but there is no evidence of architectural or engineering domain transfer from parents.

name: Gianna Nannini
milestone_by_age_26: Released her self-titled debut album in 1976 (age 22) and her second album 'Una Radura' in 1977. Her first domestic hit single 'America' and the album 'California' came in 1979 (age 25), making her a recognized figure in the Italian rock scene by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Siena to a confectionery manufacturer father (also president of Siena Football Club), Nannini studied piano at the Lucca Conservatory through her adolescence. At 19, she left home for Milan to pursue music, studying composition with Bruno Bettinelli and performing in local bars. She was first hired as a vocalist in 1974, signed to the Numero Uno label (owned by Mogol and Lucio Battisti), and released her debut album in 1976. Her breakthrough came with 'America' in 1979.
family_context_summary: Nannini was born to a family that included a renowned industrialist and Siena Football Club president father and a Formula One pilot brother (Alessandro Nannini). She has been described as the creative rebel in the family. Her father's confectionery manufacturing business provided a middle-class financial platform.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented family musical background. Her father was an industrialist (confectionery manufacturing) and her brother was a Formula One pilot. The family was wealthy but not musically connected.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Lucca Conservatory, Milan music scene, Numero Uno label, Bettinelli composition study, family rebel, debut album 1976
evidence_summary: Nannini grew up in a wealthy Siena family (father was a confectionery industrialist and Siena FC president) but was the creative rebel, leaving home at 19 for Milan. She trained at the Lucca Conservatory as a pianist and studied composition with Bruno Bettinelli in Milan. The Milan music scene of the 1970s provided a vibrant ecosystem. She signed to Numero Uno (the label of Italian pop heavyweights Mogol and Lucio Battisti) and released her debut album at 22 in 1976. Her first hit 'America' came at 25 in 1979. While her family provided financial safety, there was no musical domain transfer, and her path was largely self-driven.
